title: Score-Based Density Estimation from Pairwise Comparisons
one_liner: The paper estimates a full probability density from pairwise preference data by learning the score of the winner density and then correcting it with a position-dependent tempering field to recover the hidden belief density.
lead: Suppose an expert cannot assign numeric probabilities directly, but can repeatedly choose which of two options is preferred. Those pairwise comparisons reveal something about the expert's hidden belief density, meaning the probability density that describes which outcomes the expert finds plausible, but not in a direct way. Preferred samples are biased toward high-density regions, so the observed winner density is a distorted version of the target belief. This paper formalizes that distortion. It shows that the score of the hidden belief density and the score of the observed winner density are collinear, with the scaling determined by a position-dependent tempering field. The method then learns the winner score with score matching, estimates the tempering field under a Bradley-Terry preference model, and de-tempers the score to reconstruct the full belief density. A diffusion model trained on these corrected score signals can then sample from complex multivariate beliefs using only hundreds to thousands of pairwise comparisons.

problem.h2: Why preference data does not directly give a density
paras: A density tells you how probability mass is distributed over a continuous space. Pairwise comparison data only tells you which option won inside each pair. If one sample is chosen over another, that means the expert preferred it under some hidden preference-scoring rule, but it does not tell you the density value itself.

A naive strategy would treat the winners as direct samples from the target density and fit a generative model to them. That fails because winners are selection-biased. Regions that already have high hidden probability produce winners more often, so the winner density is more concentrated than the belief density.

The central question is therefore structural: what exact mathematical relationship links the unobserved belief density to the observed winner density? Once that link is known, density estimation becomes possible.

callout.html: The target belief density is not observed directly. What you observe is a tempered winner density whose score points in the same direction but with a position-dependent scale factor.

steps.text: Sample candidate pairs and ask an expert or preference oracle which one is preferred.
Treat the marginal density of winners as an observable target and learn its score function with score matching.
Under the Bradley-Terry model, derive or estimate the position-dependent factor that links winner score to belief score.
Divide out the tempering effect so the recovered score points in the direction of steepest increase of the hidden belief density.
Use the recovered score inside a score-based generative model or diffusion process to sample from the estimated belief density.

paras: The paper changes the estimation target from pairwise choice probabilities to the score field of a continuous density. Instead of predicting who wins each comparison only, it reconstructs the full shape of the hidden belief probability pattern.
object.object: the quantity inferred from preference data

hidden.name: position-dependent scale between winner and belief scores
paras: A score function is the direction and rate of fastest increase of the log density. It points toward increasing probability mass and tells a score-based generative model how to move samples. The paper proves that the score of the winner density and the score of the hidden belief density are aligned in direction. They differ by a multiplicative field that depends on location.

That field is hidden because pairwise comparisons do not expose it directly. Yet it is exactly what must be known to undo the preference-selection bias. If the field is greater than one in some region, the winner process has sharpened the score there more strongly; if smaller, the sharpening is weaker. Estimating this field correctly is what turns winner modeling into belief-density estimation.

heat.caption: Darker means the variable is more central to converting observed winners into a corrected hidden-density estimate.

reads.html: The winner density points in the right direction but pushes too hard in some places and not enough in others. The tempering field tells you how much to correct that push at each location.
The belief score and winner score are collinear, and the tempering field under the Bradley-Terry model provides the local scale needed for de-tempering.

mechanism.h2: Why score estimation makes this possible
paras: Score-based models do not need normalized density values. They only need the score field, which is often easier to estimate in high dimensions. That fits the preference setting because pairwise data does not naturally give normalized probabilities anyway.

The paper's first insight is to move from belief density to winner density. Winners are observable because every comparison produces one. If you aggregate those winners, you get a real density in data space. A score-matching objective can then learn how that winner density changes locally. The second insight is that, under a random utility preference model such as Bradley-Terry, the winner score is not arbitrary. It is a tempered version of the belief score. That gives a direct route back to the hidden target.

Once the corrected score is available, standard score-based sampling machinery applies. The paper uses diffusion-style training on tempered samples generated by score-scaled annealed Langevin dynamics. The important point is that pairwise comparison data is not used to supervise the final density directly. It is used to infer a score field that can drive a generative sampler.

stages.s: Pairwise comparisons from an expert or preference oracle
Aggregate winners to define the winner density
Learn winner score with score matching
Estimate tempering field under Bradley-Terry preference model
De-temper the winner score and use it in diffusion sampling

math.h2: Winner score, belief score, and de-tempering
math.words: Learn the score of the observable winner density, then divide by the local tempering field to recover the score of the hidden belief density.
math.equation: s_w(x) = tau(x) s_p(x),   so   s_p(x) = s_w(x) / tau(x)
symbols: score of the winner density at point x
score of the latent belief density at point x
position-dependent tempering field produced by the preference mechanism
a point in the continuous data space
pairwise preference model used to derive or estimate tau(x)
training objective used to fit the winner score without normalized densities

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose at a point x the learned winner score is s_w(x) = [2.0, 1.0].
The estimated tempering field there is tau(x) = 1.25.
Then the recovered belief score is s_p(x) = [1.6, 0.8].
This means the winner density and belief density point in the same direction, but the winner density has been sharpened by the preference mechanism.
A Langevin or diffusion sampler using the corrected score follows the hidden belief shape rather than the over-sharpened winner shape.

math.note: The paper's theory provides the justification for this correction. Without the tempering field, fitting winners alone would recover the wrong density.

bars.h2: What the method adds beyond direct winner modeling

charts.title: Fit density to winners directly
charts.note: This approach confuses the winner density with the belief density.

charts.title: Model comparisons only as binary outcomes
charts.note: Choice prediction alone does not recover a generative model over the expert's beliefs.

charts.title: This paper
rows: Works with hundreds to thousands of comparisons
charts.note: By estimating the winner score and de-tempering it, the method recovers a usable score field for generative sampling.

items.html: The tempering-field estimator relies on assumptions such as Bradley-Terry-style pairwise choice behavior. If the expert's selection process departs strongly from that model, the de-tempering correction can be biased.

items.b: Sparse comparisons leave the local density shape underdetermined.
items.html: In high dimensions, a small number of pairwise outcomes may not constrain the winner score well enough in all regions, especially away from frequently preferred areas.

items.b: Score estimation errors propagate into sampling.
items.html: Diffusion and Langevin procedures depend directly on the recovered score field. If the winner score or tempering field is noisy, generated samples can drift toward incorrect modes.

The method is most attractive when numeric density supervision is unavailable but pairwise preferences are cheap, because it converts those preferences into a full generative object rather than a ranking-only model.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a two-dimensional hidden target density and a preference oracle that selects winners according to a Bradley-Terry rule. Generate pairwise comparisons, fit the winner score with score matching, estimate the tempering field, and sample from the recovered belief density with Langevin or diffusion updates. Compare against a baseline that fits only the winner density. Plot both resulting sample clouds against the true target density.
demo.metric_eq: belief_error = distance(estimated_density, true_density), winner_bias = distance(winner_density, true_density)
demo.closing: The demo should show that winner samples alone are too concentrated, while de-tempering restores the broader hidden belief density.
